reference_items.proposition: Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(1)(b) supplies the directly governing statutory candidate: for conduct on or after 9 June 1952, eviction may be ordered where the tenant has sub-let, assigned, or otherwise parted with possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the landlord's consent in writing.

evidence.quote: that the tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

reference_items.relevance: This text states both sides of the fixed inquiry: there must be a qualifying subletting, assignment or parting with possession, and the statutory ground depends on absence of written landlord consent.
reference_items.limits: This is a statutory reproduction rather than an authenticated historical consolidation, and its version status expressly says the historical version is unverified. It supplies no target-specific judicial interpretation.

reference_items.proposition: Section 16 reinforces the written-consent requirement by providing that post-9 June 1952 subletting without written landlord consent is not lawful and that, after commencement of the Act, subletting or transfer or assignment of tenancy rights requires previous consent in writing.

evidence.quote: No premises which have been sub-let either in whole or in part on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord, shall be deemed to have been lawfully sub-let.

After the commencement of this Act, no tenant shall, without the previous consent in writing of the landlord, -(a) sub-let the whole or any part of the premises held by him as a tenant; or(b) transfer or assign his rights in the tenancy or in any part thereof.

reference_items.relevance: It bears directly on the appellant's contention that consent mattered but the writing requirement could be treated as merely directory.
reference_items.limits: Section 16 is statutory context rather than the stated eviction ground itself. The supplied reproduction is a current snapshot with historical-version caution, and no complete historical statute is supplied.

reference_items.proposition: The allowed target record identifies written consent as a live issue and supplies Clause 14 of the lease: the lessee undertook not to sub-let without the lessor's written permission, while the same written clause expressly stated that the lessee's contractors, M/s R.C. Abrol & Co., would share the premises with the lessor's permission.

evidence.quote: and secondly it was urged that if there was sub-letting that had been made with the written consent of the landlord. The Clause 14 of the lease deed in the instant case which provides, inter alia, the terms and conditions is as follows:-

"Clause 14-That the lessee undertakes not to sub- let the premises to any other party without the written permission of the lessor, and that the lessee's contractors M/s R.C. Abrol & Co. will share the premises with the permission of the lessor."

reference_items.relevance: Clause 14 is the strongest supplied target-specific material on written consent. It expressly permits R.C. Abrol & Co. to share the premises, so the scope of that permission is central to whether any proved occupation was consented to in writing. 粘贴的文本 (1)
reference_items.limits: The clause distinguishes a general prohibition on subletting without written permission from specific permission for R.C. Abrol & Co. to 'share' the premises. The supplied material does not establish whether the actual arrangement remained mere sharing, involved transfer of legal possession, or exceeded the permission expressed in the clause.

reference_items.proposition: Within the retrospective allowed record, the Rent Control Tribunal had findings against the tenant on the disputed subletting/parting and written-consent contentions, and the Delhi High Court affirmed those findings.

evidence.quote: The Rent Control Tribunal confirmed the findings against the appellant in all the three contentions and the High Court also affirmed the findings of the Rent Control Tribunal.

reference_items.relevance: These identified prior-court findings form part of the permitted procedural posture and show that both substantive issues had previously been resolved adversely to the tenant before the Supreme Court appeal.
reference_items.limits: The supplied allowed record does not give the underlying factual reasoning for those findings, and the target Supreme Court's final reasoning and outcome are expressly withheld. The prior findings therefore cannot be treated as the supplied Supreme Court's adopted final resolution.

reference_items.proposition: A 1986 Supreme Court judgment, General Radio, reports the earlier Parasaram decision as construing Delhi Rent Control Act section 14(b) broadly enough to cover a sublease, an assignment, or any other mode by which possession is parted, including an involuntary sale.

evidence.quote: On appeal by special leave this Court held that the amplitude of S. 14(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act was wide enough not only to include any sublease but even an assignment or any other mode by which possession of the tenanted premises is parted. In view of the wide amplitude of s. 14(b), it does not exclude even an involuntary sale.

reference_items.relevance: This supplied Supreme Court report supports a broad reading of the kinds of transfers capable of falling within section 14(1)(b), so the inquiry is not limited to a formally labelled sublease.
reference_items.limits: The library expressly classifies this as a reported precedent and not the independently supplied full Parasaram opinion. Its facts concerned a liquidation sale, and it does not by itself establish what counts as parting with legal possession when a named contractor merely shares premises with the tenant.

reference_items.proposition: The tenant's Supreme Court argument was that landlord consent was mandatory but the requirement that consent be proved in writing was merely directory.

evidence.quote: it was not necessary that the consent to sub-letting should be in writing and what he contended was that it was necessary to have the consent and the manner of proving consent was provided in writing.
the provision which required that the consent should be in writing meant it was mandatory so far as it enjoined consent but it was directory so far as it said that such consent should be in writing.

reference_items.relevance: This is the supplied opposing construction of the written-consent element and therefore identifies a concrete dispute that must be tested against sections 14(1)(b) and 16.
reference_items.limits: It is counsel's submission only. The supplied target record does not state that the Supreme Court adopted it, while the supplied statutory language repeatedly uses 'consent in writing' and 'previous consent in writing'.

analysis_points: The supplied statutory materials support eviction under the fixed ground only if the relevant conduct qualifies as subletting, assignment or other parting with possession and occurred without the landlord's written consent. The statute therefore leaves two distinct substantive questions: what possession was actually transferred, and whether that transaction was covered by written consent.

Clause 14 materially supports the tenant on the consent side because it is itself a writing and expressly says that M/s R.C. Abrol & Co. 'will share the premises with the permission of the lessor.' Its effect depends on whether the alleged occupation was the permitted sharing contemplated by the clause or a materially different subletting, assignment or parting with legal possession.

The permitted lower-court history shows adverse findings against the tenant on both subletting/parting and consent, but the allowed record does not disclose the factual basis for those findings, and the Supreme Court's final reasoning and outcome are withheld. Those prior findings may be recorded as procedural facts but cannot supply the missing target final reasoning.

The reported Parasaram interpretation supports a broad conception of section 14(b), extending beyond formal subleases to assignments and other modes of parting with possession. It does not resolve the decisive target-specific distinction between permitted shared occupation by a contractor and a transfer of legal possession.

On the supplied material alone, there is source-grounded support for an eviction theory if the tenant actually surrendered legal possession to R.C. Abrol & Co. beyond the lease's permitted sharing and lacked written consent for that transaction; there is also source-grounded resistance to eviction if the arrangement amounted only to the expressly permitted sharing. The decisive facts needed to choose between those characterizations are not supplied.
gaps: The allowed record does not describe the actual possession arrangement with R.C. Abrol & Co.: it does not state who retained keys, control, access, ability to exclude others, day-to-day dominion, or whether any portion was placed in R.C. Abrol & Co.'s exclusive possession.

The record does not establish whether the alleged actionable arrangement was exactly the 'share the premises' arrangement authorized in Clause 14 or whether its nature later changed or exceeded that written permission.

The date on which the alleged subletting, assignment or parting with possession occurred is not supplied, so the statutory temporal condition referring to conduct on or after 9 June 1952 cannot independently be verified from the allowed target record.

The target cites Vishwa Nath, Gurdial Singh, Reliable Finance Corporation and Madras Bangalore Transport Co. in support of the no-parting-of-legal-possession argument, but the supplied target record gives only their names and counsel's characterization; their actual holdings and limits are not supplied in the common legal library and therefore cannot be adopted as reference propositions.

The Delhi statutory reproductions are expressly marked as current snapshots with historical versions unverified, so the precise authenticated statutory text applicable on the target date is not independently established by the supplied library.
disputes: Whether R.C. Abrol & Co.'s occupation amounted merely to permitted sharing or instead to subletting, assignment, or parting with legal possession within section 14(1)(b).

Whether Clause 14's written permission for R.C. Abrol & Co. to share the premises constitutes the required written landlord consent for the actual arrangement proved, or whether that permission was narrower than the alleged transfer of possession.

Whether the statutory requirement that landlord consent be 'in writing' can be treated as directory, as the tenant argued, despite the supplied text of sections 14(1)(b) and 16 expressly requiring written or previous written consent.
How much weight may be given to the adverse Tribunal and High Court findings when their supporting factual reasoning is absent and the Supreme Court's withheld final reasoning may not be inferred.
